1: John's vision of the risen Christ

On the island of Patmos, on the Lord's day, John hears a voice like a trumpet and sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, his face shining like the sun. He says, "Fear not. I am the first and the last, and the living one."
The book opens with Christ alive and in the midst of his churches. Its purpose is to give courage.
2: Christ speaks to Ephesus, which has lost its first love; to Smyrna, poor and persecuted; to Pergamum, which tolerates false teaching; and to Thyatira, which tolerates a false prophetess. Each letter ends with a promise to the one who conquers.
Christ knows each community exactly, its good and its bad. He corrects in order to save.
3: Sardis has a reputation for being alive but is dead. Philadelphia has little power but has kept his word. Laodicea is lukewarm, neither hot nor cold. "Behold, I stand at the door and knock."
Comfort can be more dangerous than persecution. Christ knocks; he waits to be let in.
4: A door opens in heaven. John sees a throne with a rainbow around it, twenty-four elders, and four living creatures who never stop singing, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty."
Before any trouble is shown, John sees who is in charge. The Sanctus at Mass echoes this song.
5: No one is worthy to open the sealed scroll in God's hand, and John weeps. Then he sees a Lamb standing as though slain. The Lamb takes the scroll, and all heaven worships him.
History is in the hands of the crucified and risen Christ. The Lamb receives the same worship as God.
6: The Lamb opens the seals. Four horsemen ride out, bringing conquest, war, famine and death. The martyrs under the altar cry, "How long?" The sixth seal shakes heaven and earth.
The evils of history are real, but they are limited and not the last word. God hears the martyrs.
7: The sealed and the countless crowd

God's servants are sealed, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a multitude no one can count, from every nation, in white robes with palm branches. They have come through the great tribulation.
This is read on All Saints' Day. Heaven is full of people from everywhere, and God will wipe away every tear.
8: The seventh seal and the trumpets
There is silence in heaven. An angel offers incense with the prayers of the saints. Four trumpets sound, and a third of the earth, sea, rivers and sky are struck.
The prayers of God's people rise before him and matter in his plan.
9: The fifth trumpet releases locusts from the abyss that torment people for five months. The sixth releases a vast army. Yet the survivors do not repent of their idols or their crimes.
The plagues are warnings meant to turn people back. Hearts can stay hard even then.
10: A mighty angel gives John a small scroll to eat. It is sweet as honey in his mouth and bitter in his stomach. He is told he must prophesy again.
God's word is sweet to receive and hard to carry and proclaim.
11: Two witnesses and the seventh trumpet

Two witnesses prophesy, are killed by the beast, and are raised by God. The seventh trumpet sounds: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord." The ark of the covenant is seen in heaven.
Faithful witness can look like defeat and end in victory.
12: A woman clothed with the sun, crowned with twelve stars, gives birth to a son who will rule the nations. A great red dragon tries to devour him. Michael and his angels throw the dragon down. The dragon then makes war on the woman's other children.
The Church sees in the woman both God's people and Mary, mother of the Messiah. Satan is already a defeated enemy.
13: A beast rises from the sea with power from the dragon, and the world worships it. A second beast makes people worship the first and marks them with its number, 666.
The beasts stand for political power that demands worship and the propaganda that serves it. Christians must refuse to adore any state or ruler.
14: The Lamb stands with the 144,000, who sing a new song. Angels announce the eternal Gospel and the fall of Babylon. "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord." The earth is harvested.
Those who stay faithful are with the Lamb. Their deeds follow them.
15: Those who conquered the beast stand beside a sea of glass and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Seven angels receive seven bowls of God's wrath.
As Israel sang after the Red Sea, the saved praise God's justice.
16: The bowls are poured out: sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat, darkness, the Euphrates dried up, and a great earthquake. The kings gather at Armageddon. People curse God instead of repenting.
God's judgements are just. Evil finally destroys itself.
17: An angel shows John a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, seated on a beast, drunk with the blood of the saints. She is the great city that rules the kings of the earth, and her own allies will turn on her.
For John's first readers this meant pagan Rome. It stands for every society built on luxury, idolatry and persecution.
18: An angel cries, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!" Kings, merchants and sailors weep because no one buys their cargo any more. God's people are told, "Come out of her."
Wealth built on injustice does not last. Christians are not to share in its sins.
19: Heaven shouts "Alleluia". The marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride is ready. Then a rider on a white horse, called Faithful and True, the Word of God, defeats the beast and its armies.
"Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb" is said at every Mass. Christ wins.
20: The thousand years and the last judgement
Satan is bound for a thousand years, released for a last revolt, and thrown into the lake of fire. The dead, great and small, stand before a great white throne and are judged by what they have done.
The Church reads the thousand years as the present age of Christ's reign, not a future earthly kingdom. Every life will be judged.
21: A new heaven and a new earth

The holy city, the new Jerusalem, comes down from God like a bride. God will live with his people; death, mourning and pain will be no more. The city has twelve gates and needs no sun, because the Lamb is its lamp.
"Behold, I make all things new." The goal of history is God dwelling with us.
22: The river of the water of life flows from the throne, and the tree of life bears fruit every month. God's servants will see his face. Jesus says, "I am coming soon." The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come."
The Bible that began in a garden ends in a garden city. Its last prayer is for Christ to come.
